question_text: Choose the correct transitional word: 'The project was delayed ___ budget constraints.'

hint_ladder.title: Look at what follows the blank
hint_ladder.text: The words after the blank are 'budget constraints.' Is that a full sentence with a verb, or just a thing? It's a noun phrase — just a thing, no action.

hint_ladder.title: The simple rule
hint_ladder.text: Some words (like 'because' and 'since') need a full clause after them — a subject and a verb. Others (like 'because of') can work with just a noun phrase.

hint_ladder.title: Test each option
hint_ladder.text: Try saying the sentence with each option. 'Because budget constraints' sounds incomplete, right? 'Because of budget constraints' flows naturally. 'Since budget constraints' also feels unfinished. 'Due budget constraints' is missing a word.

hint_ladder.title: Spot the only one that fits
hint_ladder.text: Only one option is a compound preposition that can smoothly introduce a noun phrase. The others either need a full clause or need another word ('to') to work.

A.text: This is a very common mistake. 'Because' is a conjunction, which means it needs to introduce a full clause — a group of words with a subject and a verb, like 'because there were budget constraints.' Here, 'budget constraints' is just a noun phrase with no verb, so 'because' alone doesn't work. Your brain might have jumped to the most familiar reason word, but the structure after it matters just as much.

B.text: Perfect choice. 'Because of' is a compound preposition, which means it can smoothly introduce a noun phrase like 'budget constraints.' Think of it as the go-to phrase when you want to give a reason but don't have a full sentence after it. It's like the bridge that connects the delay to the reason without needing extra words.

C.text: 'Since' is another conjunction, just like 'because.' It also needs a full clause after it — for example, 'since the budget was constrained.' Without a verb, 'since budget constraints' feels incomplete. It's easy to pick 'since' because it sounds similar in meaning, but the grammar rule is the same: conjunctions need clauses.

D.text: This one is tricky because 'due to' is a perfectly correct phrase. But here, 'due' is standing alone without its partner 'to.' 'Due' by itself is an adjective, not a preposition, so it can't introduce a noun phrase. If the option were 'due to,' it would be correct. Always check if 'to' is there — it's a common trap in exams.

next_time_rule: Quick test: If the word after the blank is a noun phrase (no verb), use 'because of' or 'due to.' If it's a full clause (subject + verb), use 'because' or 'since.'
blueprint_id: Transitional Words — Because vs Because Of
deconstruct_text: Let's walk through this together. The sentence is: 'The project was delayed ___ budget constraints.' The key is to look at what comes after the blank. 'Budget constraints' is a noun phrase — it's just a thing, with no action or verb. Now, some words can introduce a noun phrase, and some can't. 'Because' and 'since' are conjunctions — they need a full clause after them, like 'because there were budget constraints' or 'since the budget was tight.' Without a verb, they leave the sentence hanging. 'Due' is an adjective that needs 'to' to become the preposition 'due to.' So 'due' alone is incomplete. That leaves 'because of,' which is a compound preposition designed exactly for this job — introducing a noun phrase that explains a reason. It's like the perfect key for this lock. Here's a mental trick I want you to remember: Think of 'because of' as the phrase you use when you're giving a one-word or short reason. 'Because' is for when you need a whole story. 'Because of rain' works. 'Because it rained' works. Mix them up, and the sentence feels off.
